options: Where FILTERS (keeps matching items); Select TRANSFORMS (each item becomes something else)
explanation: Where: same items, fewer of them. Select: same count, different shape. The two halves of most queries.

stem: Nothing matches. pupils.First(p => p.Mark > 99) versus FirstOrDefault:
options: First THROWS InvalidOperationException; FirstOrDefault returns null/default
explanation: Choose by meaning: FirstOrDefault when absence is normal (then null-check); First when absence would be a bug worth hearing about.

stem: When would you use Single(...) instead of First(...)?
options: When TWO matches would mean corrupt data - Single throws on duplicates, First silently takes one
explanation: Single asserts exactly-one: find-by-unique-id is the classic case. First shrugs at extras.

options: Max gives the highest MARK (an int); MaxBy gives the PUPIL who has it
explanation: Wanting the top scorer and reaching for Max then searching again is the long way round - MaxBy returns the item directly.

options: Any STOPS at the first item; Count walks the entire sequence
explanation: On a lazy or large source that difference is real work. Any(predicate) similarly stops at the first match.

stem: Where before Select in a chain is preferred because:
options: You TRANSFORM FEWER items - filter first, then shape survivors
explanation: Both orders can be correct; filtering first does less work. Same instinct scales up in 3.7's reports.
Keep >2 (5, 8), order (5, 8), times ten (50, 80). Reading a chain top to bottom like a sentence is the skill.
Skip past two full pages (20 items), take the next 10. Take-then-Skip would slice the wrong end.

stem: Sorting by subject, ties broken by mark descending:
explanation: ThenBy adds a tiebreak; a second OrderBy would REPLACE the first ordering entirely - a classic silent bug.

stem: from p in pupils where p.Year == 10 select p.Name - versus method syntax:
options: IDENTICAL meaning - two spellings of the same query
explanation: The compiler translates query syntax into the same Where/Select calls. Read both; write whichever is clearer for the query at hand.
